speechtext:
The committee will be, I am sure, not only interested in learning but pleased to know that the government has been successful in enlisting the good offices of Mr. Leighton McCarthy at this particular time, and that Mr. McCarthy has been appointed as minister to Washington. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition mentioned last night that he thought we should have at Washington at this time an outstanding citizen of Canada, and he linked Mr. Leighton McCarthy's name to the designation which he had given, so I am happy to feel that on this occasion both sides of the house are of one view with respect to our good fortune-I call it such advisedly-in securing Mr. McCarthy's services as minister.
Perhaps I should tell the committee that some years ago I tried to get Mr. McCarthy to take the office of minister at Washington. Mr. McCarthy could not see his way at the time to sever his business connection in Canada to the extent of giving himself to the diplomatic service. He has indicated to me off and on since the war began that if he could be of service in any way he would be glad to consider any proposal that might be made to him. As soon as I found that Mr. Christie's recovery would unfortunately likely take some time, I got in touch with Mr. McCarthy and, after having considered the matter carefully, he has agreed to accept the position of minister for such time as he is able to give his services at Washington.
As hon. members know, Mr. McCarthy is a former member of this House of Commons. He took a prominent part in the discussion of public affairs when he was a member of parliament. He is head of one of the largest insurance companies in Canada and has had a great deal to do with private business. He has also an exceptionally high standing in his own profession, that of the law. He has always been interested in international affairs. With respect to his appointment to Washington there is a circumstance which I believe to be of real value to us all; it is that Mr. McCarthy and the president of the United States have been very close friends for many years and know each other intimately. I feel that no better appointment to Washington could possibly have been made.
Some little time ago the Prime Minister of Great Britain communicated with me with regard to a possible appointment to the imperial privy council and discussed the qualifications which he felt should govern in the appointment of a privy councillor. Mr. Churchill set forth the following condition and qualification which I pass on to the committee as exceptionally valuable, whether 14873-644
made applicable to the position of privy councillor in Britain or in any of the dominions. The position, Mr. Churchill said, should be regarded not as being bestowed as an honour or as a reward, but as the sworn relationship deemed necessary for the performance of highly confidential duties by persons of eminent stations. The government has felt that Mr. McCarthy's relationship with itself would be one involving the performance of highly confidential duties and he would certainly be recognized as enjoying an eminent station. The cabinet therefore recommended to his excellency the appointment of Mr. McCarthy as a member of the privy council of Canada. His excellency has been pleased to approve the recommendation. Mr. McCarthy, therefore, goes to Washington not merely as a minister but also as a member of the privy council of Canada.
Recognizing the importance of the work to be done at Washington, and in order to give Mr. McCarthy the best assistance we possibly can, the Department of External Affairs has arranged to have Mr. Hume Wrong accompany Mr. McCarthy when he goes to Washington. Hon. members will recall that Mr. Wrong was associated with the legation at Washington for ten years altogether, and he is therefore familiar with the Washington scene and has many friends in the different departments of government there. Mr. Wrong has been at the League of Nations as permanent delegate from Canada. That particular position has been abandoned for obvious reasons. Since October, 1939, he has been special economic adviser in London, dealing more particularly with matters of economic warfare and with financial questions. He is therefore familiar with many aspects of the situation in London and will bring that added knowledge to the discharge of his duties in Washington at this time.
As I mentioned on Monday a week ago, the affairs of the legation, during Mr. Christie's unfortunate illness, have been administered by Mr. Merchant Mahoney as charge d'affaires. I doubt if a more faithful, honourable or efficient officer could be found in any public service than Mr. Mahoney has been in the years he has been at Washington. In fact, if I recollect rightly, he was first appointed to Washington some time before the legation was opened. He was appointed as representative of the imperial munitions board. He has made for himself a place of exceptional confidence in Washington and he will continue, of course, as counsellor at the legation. The government feels, however, that he should be given a higher rank than he is at present enjoying. He is at present commercial counsellor, but his duties have taken him outside
Supply-External Affairs

purely commercial lines into general problems of government and matters of general concern; his responsibilities have long ago outrun the limited description of his duties conveyed by the title "commercial counsellor" and he has therefore the position of counsellor of legation without qualification.
Mr. Wrong will be the senior counsellor, having had exceptional experience in international affairs in many parts of the world, but I should like the committee to realize 4hat this country owes a very great debt of gratitude to Mr. Merchant Mahoney for the way in which he has supported all ministers who have been in Washington and the very unselfish role which he has taken at all times in serving this country there.
I feel I should place on the record an exchange of correspondence which has taken place between Mr. Christie and myself, so that the committee will know exactly the position as it stands at the present time, and as it relates to the future. On February 19, Mr. Christie wrote to me from the Hospital of the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, 66th street and York avenue, New York, as follows:
My dear Prime Minister:
I have now learned from my doctors that my full recovery is likely to take somewhat longer than they thought and I had hoped. My absence from Washington, particularly in these very difficult times, has been very much on my mind and I know it has caused you concern. I had expected to be able to take up my full duties at the legation before this, but I quite realize that, with a convalescence in prospect that may take some months, the vital interests of Canada in Washington cannot be adequately maintained without full and effective diplomatic representation there.
In all the circumstances I hope it may be found possible to grant me the extended leave of absence from the legation which I am told I must have in order to complete my recovery. I hope you will therefore, feel entirely free to make whatever arrangements in respect of the Canadian legation at Washington the needs of the country and the service may require.
Yours very sincerely,
Loring C. Christie.
To Mr. Christie's communication I replied on February 20 as follows:
Office of the Prime Minister Canada
Ottawa, February 20, 1941.
My dear Christie:
I am more than sorry to learn that you now feel your complete recovery may take rather longer than we had all hoped. I know that your enforced absence from your post in this critical period has been an added source of anxiety which no doubt has been impeding your recovery.
It is characteristic of your thoughtfulness in all that pertains to the public service to suggest that your present indisposition should not be allowed to impair in any way the effective representation of Canada at Washington,
{Mr. Mackenzie King.]
especially in time of war. Anticipating that such would be your attitude once you found that time would be required for a complete restoration of your health, I had, prior to the receipt of your letter, been considering what steps it might be most advisable to take for the effective carrying on of the work of the legation in the event of a prolonged absence on your part being necessary.
It is, I think, desirable that you should take an extended leave of absence so that you can enjoy the complete rest which your recovery requires, and which your services to Canada, both at home and abroad, have amply earned. It is also most important that the representative of Canada at Washington should, particularly at this time, be someone who will have the complete authority and status of a minister. This I have reason to believe can be arranged without impairing your own status as a minister in Canada's diplomatic service.
I much hope that procedure on these lines may serve to relieve your mind of all present anxieties and enable the government at a later date again to avail itself of your exceptional talents wherever they may be utilized to the best advantage.
With kindest regards to yourself and with every wish for an early and complete restoration of your health,
Believe me,
Yours very sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King. Loring C. Christie, Esq.,
Rockefeller Institute,
New York, N.Y.
I should have said at the outset that His Majesty the King was of course duly advised of the wishes of the government with respect to the appointment of Mr. McCarthy to Washington, and has been pleased to signify his approval of the appointment and of the course it was proposed to adopt with respect thereto. I mention this because a procedure somewhat different from that which is customary has been adopted in the case of Mr. McCarthy going to Washington. As a rule, a new minister presents the letters of recall of his predecessor and his own letter of credence. But as Mr. Christie will remain a minister, although absent, it has not been thought necessary to have Mr. McCarthy present any letters of recall or letters of credence. The President of the United States and the Secretary of State are agreed that an oral communication by Mr. McCarthy on his arrival, to the president who understands the special situation and approves of the arrangement contemplated, will suffice. Mr. Roosevelt, who, as I have already mentioned, knows Mr. McCarthy very well, has informed me that he will be only too pleased to receive Mr. McCarthy with the full authority and status of minister the moment he arrives in Washington, without any special letter of credence from His Majesty the King. The arrangements for Canadian representation at Washington I hope are of a character which

Supply-External Affairs
will meet all the needs of the situation at the present time. I trust they may also prove of benefit to the health of Mr. Christie, who is an exceptionally able and faithful public servant.

The Prime Minister has made some very interesting announcements. I cannot suppose that the advance notice of the appointment of Mr. McCarthy that I gave here the other day was unknown to the Prime Minister, because it had already been announced in the Toronto newspapers, but I do think the Prime Minister has made a very good choice.
I am pleased to know that he has created Mr. McCarthy a privy councillor. I had hoped that he might give consideration to the suggestion which I made in perfect good faith, that it being the most important post in our diplomatic service, he might see his way clear to raise the new minister to the rank of ambassador, because I do think that would enhance his importance in Washington at least one degree. The Prime Minister has not seen fit to do that, and of course I make no further comment.
Since he announced the appointment of Mr. McCarthy as privy councillor, I have been wondering whether consideration has been given to the suggestion, made to me at all events, that our high commissioner in Australia, for instance, should be made a privy councillor. I am told that it not only carries something with it as a matter of dignity but carries with it certain rights of access to the Prime Minister or the cabinet in person. I just mention this in passing because I understood that it has been the practice on previous occasions to make our high commissioners, as well as some at least of our ministers abroad, privy councillors. The former Prime Minister made Mr. Howard Ferguson a privy councillor, also Mr. Herridge, and I am thinking of my friend C. J. Burchell, the high commissioner in Australia. Could he not be made a privy councillor? I am not going to carry the suggestion any further than that.
With what the Prime Minister said about Mr. Hume Wrong I concur. I have had the pleasure of meeting Mr. Wrong in Washington, and from the efforts he made to assist me as a private individual, I learned of his competence as an official. I can say the same thing for Mr. Mahoney. He knows his way about in Washington; he is a valuable official of the Canadian legation there, and I am indeed pleased to see this recognition given to him. I think it is perhaps somewhat long delayed on the part of Canada to a man who has served this country so well. He was sent down there by Sir Robert Borden, if my
recollection is correct, at a time when we had1 no actual representation in Washington, and! during the last war he did useful work for Canada, as I am sure he has done since.

What I have-been most anxious to avoid, particularly at this time of war, was any question being: raised which might give rise to general discussion as to what might lie back of any particular step. While I have never even replied to the insinuations that because I was a stalwart Canadian I therefore could not be equally staunch as a supporter of the British empire, I have carefully endeavoured to avoid taking any steps that might lead to misunderstanding and misrepresentation. I have just had to ask myself the question, how would some people in this country view a step which would create an embassy at Washington at this particular moment? Personally I feel that there are the strongest reasons why we should have an embassy at Washington. I believe in the equality of status of all the self-governing nations of the-British empire. And the fact that we have had' a legation at Washington rather than an embassy has been due not to any inferiority complex, but rather to a sense of proportion] in the beginnings of our diplomatic services.
I shall explore the matter further, but at: what time it may be best to take the step-that has been suggested1 I think will have to-be carefully considered.
As to the creation of privy councillors, incommon with my hon. friend, I should be happy to see a number of our friends recog-
Supply-External Affairs

nized as members of the privy council. I feel however, that that is one particular office which should be reserved as largely as possible for those who have had immediate experience or large experience in matters of government which, as I have said, Mr. Churchill feels should be the relationship to entitle anyone to that position. I talked with Mr. Baldwin when he was in Canada about the position of privy councillors in England. He said to me that in his opinion there was no position which should be as closely guarded as that of appointment to the privy council, that it would lose its character altogether if men, simply because they were appointed to one office, should feel that because they got that office they should therefore get the other.
It is not any lack of appreciation of the fine qualities of the men who represent us as high commissioners which causes me to hesitate to do for one what I could not do for all, or probably would be called upon to do for all, were I to make a recommendation in any one direction. I feel that the position [DOT]of high commissioner in itself is a very honourable one, and I am sure that today anyone holding that office would at all times have access to the government of the country to which he might be sent.

As my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition has just said, he called on me at my office and brought to my attention the circumstances which he has just narrated to the committee and made the suggestion that the government should consider making an appropriation of $1,000,000 or some other amount to aid in relieving distress arising from air raids in Great Britain. I said to my hon. friend that I appreciated his motives and shared his feelings with respect to the desirability of relieving distress, and that from the government's point of view it was all a question of how best to effect the end which we shared in common.
Canada's war effort need not be restricted to contributions that come from the federal parliament. Contributions may come from the provincial legislatures or from municipalities, and there may be contributions from individuals. I am using the word "contribution" in a very broad sense. I told my hon. friend that I would bring the matter to the attention of my colleagues in the cabinet and see that it received careful consideration there. In a word, the view that the cabinet took of the matter was this: that under the war appropriation bill a contribution is being made from Canada's treasury of at least $1,300,000,000 which is immediately concerned with the war effort. It might seem a simple matter to add another million or so to that amount but if we were to do so we would be establishing a precedent which perhaps would lead to many requests for donations to other special objects. We would, moreover, be departing from what seems to have been the method adopted in other parts of the empire in making contributions for this particular purpose. In London,
for example, there is the Lord Mayor's Fund. In Montreal there has recently been opened a fund with which Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth has graciously consented to have her name associated. My hon. friend has referred to what has been done in Toronto. He has spoken of Australia, but has told us the contributions were made by the cities of Melbourne and Sydney.
If I am not mistaken, the city of Ottawa made a contribution a short time ago. It is a form of relief which, if given through the municipalities, appeals immediately to the citizens generally. That would seem to be an avenue through which contributions might be made to this end, which contributions in the long run would amount to as considerable a figure as anything that the federal government itself might contribute. I venture to say that if I were to announce to-night that the federal government was going to make a contribution to this particular fund, immediately it would be found that many persons in the municipalities who otherwise would have contributed to the fund would say: "Oh, well, the federal government is making a contribution, so why should we?" Similarly, municipalities which might be anxious to associate their efforts with the efforts of other municipalities might feel that the dominion government was making a large contribution and, therefore, that it was not necessary that they should do so.
I am giving to the committee the view which the members of the government took of the matter, we being just as anxious as my hon. friend and all other hon. members to contribute to every phase of the war effort to which we could justifiably make a contribution. At this time when a campaign is in progress urging the people of this country to invest in war savings certificates, I think many persons would feel that, since that campaign was gathering up small contributions to help meet the very large obligations which the federal government has assumed, we would be more justified, in relation to this particular purpose, in leaving it to the municipalities to supplement what the federal government is doing.
I do not say that the government will not consider the matter further. If I thought that the House of Commons generally took a different view from that of the government I would very gladly ask my colleagues to reconsider the decision which we have reached. I have given briefly to hon. members the point of view which we entertained. While the matter need not be regarded as finally closed, that is the present position of the administration towards the suggestion my hon. friend has made.

As the situation is now, we are able to give a reply immediately to any communications of the kind for the simple reason that the cabinet is together in Ottawa; I can consult my colleagues in a very few minutes and we can reach our decision in no time, unless the matter be one that requires considerable discussion. get the consensus of view much more quickly than could be done by cabling from England to get possibly one set of views here and then trying to reconcile them, say with different opinions held by the government representative in London.

speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister on what basis young Canadians are selected for service in the Department of External Affairs? We seem to have recruited a number of remarkably able young men, one of the ablest perhaps being the acting under-secretary of state, Mr. Norman Robertson, who sits before the Prime Minister at the present moment, and who is a distinguished graduate of our university of British Columbia. maintopic: QUESTION AS TO PRICES AND QUANTITIES SOLD SINCE AUGUST 1
speechtext:
The Department of External Affairs is one part of the general civil service, and admission to the department, if I may use that expression, comes about in the same way as it does in other departments of government, namely, upon examinations which are fixed by the civil service commission. The department makes known its needs by applying to the commission; those who wish to enter the department send in their applications. When the time comes for an examination they take the examination. As I understand it, the examinations are not confined merely to those which are written. There are oral examinations, and the deputy minister of the department has acted with other members of the public service as an examiner at oral examinations with

Supply-External Affairs
a view of sizing up some of the qualifications of candidates which might not be apparent through the written examination.
The department does draw candidates from all parts of Canada and from all of the universities. Care has been taken, I believe, by the universities to make it known to students that there are opportunities in the government service in the Department of External Affairs.
The work of the department is pretty generally known. Those who are taking courses such as economics and political science at the universities and the young men and young women who are interested in foreign affairs send in their applications to the department. I suppose that hardly a week and never a month passes when I do not receive some communication asking how an individual can get into the department; and the same is true, of course, to a much greater extent with the deputy head. The department has a large waiting list of names of those who desire to try the examinations, also a list of those who have passed; and as opportunity arises, those who have passed the examinations are drafted into the service.
I think I ought to say, and I am sure my hon. friend would wish me to say, that the late Doctor Skelton, having held at one time the position which he did at Queens university, having taken the interest that he did at all times in students, made a point of endeavouring to discover young men in different parts of the country who would be well suited to the Canadian public service. He did what he could to encourage the best of them to try the examinations and, as far as he could, enlisted their services subsequently.
I should like to add that I agree with my hon. friend in all that he said about the acting under-secretary of state. I congratulate his university upon having sent to the public service of Canada one who lends distinction to the university as well as to himself.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO PRICES AND QUANTITIES SOLD SINCE AUGUST 1
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has given an account of this famous department of his, the Department of External Affairs. I have read all the discussions in Hansard during the many years since this department was established, and in my opinion its establishment is one of the many reasons why we have the present war. Away back at the time of the treaty of Versailles the government of the day set up this department. In an address on May 26, 1938, I gave a summary of the circumstances of its origin and the functions proposed for it, and its history and the separate acts proposed under it.
Immediately after the great war the League of Nations was established as a part of the treaty of Versailles. Great Britain agreed to
this at the behest of President Wilson, and the league was established, but without obtaining the ratification of the senate of the United States, and they refused to endorse it.
The Canadian government proceeded then to make and sign treaties separately, and so signed the halibut treaty. They insisted on a separate seat at the League of Nations; they claimed the right to separate representation at Washington and a separate embassy in the United States, for what purpose? To appease Washington. I would be the last person to say anything against the government in Washington, but Washington is quite capable of looking after its own affairs; that is a primary function of good government on the part of our kinsmen there, to protect and look after their own interests, first and last. I would that Canada would look after its own affairs as successfully.
As regards these amateur ambassadors whom we send over the seven seas, I have consistently opposed that policy. Who instructs them, and what is Canada's foreign policy? I am the only member who has opposed separate embassies and the dividing of Great Britain's representation at Washington and other capitals in the seven seas; and I did so because I believed that it would inevitably lead to division and drifting away from the mother country. We have seen the results. Hitler was thus led to believe that the dominions would not back up the mother country. In 1914 a similar thing happened, in the days of the kaiser, when we were slow to see the way the great dominions were drifting away from the empire.
As I look over the items of expenditure, which have increased herein by leaps and bounds, I ask, what are the functions of these so-called diplomats and who instructs them? They are just a lot of amateurs and only learn by experience. The ablest diplomats we have had in the history of the British empire are the permanent civil servants sent out by the foreign office; I will give the committee some names. Instead of the type of politician whom we have had representing us for the past seven years, Britain had its ablest ambassadors at Washington before and after the great war, men like Lord Pauncefote, Sir Esme Howard, Sir Robert Lindsay, and the war-time ambassador, Sir Cecil Spring-Rice, who was succeeded by two British cabinet ministers and politicians with no diplomatic experience, Lord Reading and Sir Auckland Geddes. True, the papers did not write up these skilled diplomats I first named as they do the politicians appointed.
I have opposed and still oppose the principle upon which this vote is based of dividing
Supply-External Affairs

Britain's representation. Are we or are we not a part of the British empire? If we are, why do we seek, as we have sought ever since this department was created, to divide Britain's representations in external affairs. That sort of thing is very largely what has caused this war. It led to trouble as soon as the department was created. We have heard much talk about "Canada a nation". Yes, it was a nation, as I said ten years ago, on the front pages of United States magazines and at five o'clock teas and ten o'clock dinners at Washington. We were a nation, all right, then, but we were a pauper in actual performance of paying for a fleet to defend our shores. What happened? We sent a whole lot of novice ambassadors down there, with the result that the politicians in the senate and house of representatives put it all over them in diplomacy. Now we are dumb, dumb as an oyster; we have been afraid, during these past three or four years, to say one word about what is going on in the senate and in congress, criticizing Britain and her dominions at the seat of government, and so have contributed something to the conditions which led to war. Canada has kept silent and not replied to all the four years' attacks there on the mother country before this war.
As I have said, one consequence of the creation of this department was to divide Britain's representation, and to lead Hitler to believe, as once the kaiser believed, that the dominions would not support the mother country any longer. It is a phase of separatism and isolation from the mother country, with the result that for a year or two prior to the present war the dominions were a drag on Great Britain. I say this advisedly. For the last three or four years, as this discussion has come up, I have given my personal opinion. A great French prime minister once said "You can never deal with Great Britain with regard to any treaty, because she has always to consult five or six overseas dominions, with the result that when the case has been studied, they can never reach any agreement." What he stated has proved to be correct.
Take the case of Japan, our old and faithful ally. I notice that part of the present vote, item 37, for these various embassies relates to Japan. What happened with Japan? To appease the United States the government has driven Japan into the German orbit by the Washington treaty of 1921. During the great war Japan looked after the whole of the Pacific ocean, enabling Britain to turn her back on the Pacific. Japan looked after China, the Indian empire, the six hundred miles of Canada's western coast, and as far east as the gulf of Aden and the entrance to the

Mediterranean, with the result that as far as Canada is concerned, our interests, including our shipping in the Pacific, were safeguarded.
In the great war to which I have referred, Germany kept the whole civilized world at bay for four and one-half years, although we had then as our devoted allies Italy and Japan, and, during part of the time, the United States and Russia.
This is going to be a long drawn out war and diplomacy will play a very important part in it. We have seen how, largely by diplomatic means, Germany has swept through the Norwegian and the Baltic countries, the Netherlands, the low countries and others. The speed of it shocked the people of the United States and Canada.
I repeat that I am and always have been opposed to the principle on which this vote is based. It divided our empire. It drove Japan, for thirty years our faithful ally, out of the alliance. Two years ago, when these estimates were up for discussion, we declared that Canada's defence and external affairs policy were based on two things: first, home defence, and, second, to protect our neutrality provided a foreign foe invaded our territory on its way to attack the United States. These were the two cardinal principles. Take Italy. As a result of our becoming a nation overnight we passed sanctions against Italy with respect to Ethiopia, and then all of a sudden, in three months' time, those sanctions were rescinded, with the result that Italy, an old ally and a loyal friend of ours, was driven into the German orbit. We did propose a few years ago to establish another embassy in Italy, but it was not consummated.
With regard to the other part of the discussion, I suggest that we have here another means of separating our representation in the action that has been taken in respect of the present French government. The British government has recognized the provisional government of General de Gaulle as an ally, and Australia followed three months ago in the recognition of de Gaulle as an ally, asking the Vichy representative to go home. Canada is divided on the question. Here we find Britain with one policy and Canada with another. Australia and New Zealand have a different policy from ours, and side with Britain. Vichy is doing Hitler's work and bidding and we should close it up in Canada.
A part of this vote is for the purpose of maintaining a sort of dominion embassy in Dublin to Eire. In my opinion, the Canadian people are opposed to this idea. We are spending $30,000 of this vote on this particular work, while our shipping is in a very precarious state owing to the actions of German

Supply-External Affairs
submarines and bombers in the vicinity of Irish ports on the west and northwest coasts of Ireland. We are spending, I say, a considerable part of this vote for the maintenance of a sort of embassy in what is not a British dominion but a separate republic, and a neutral. Why should we spend money over there, while Britain has her hands tied behind her back by the loss of the use of these bases, and shipping and tonnage are being sent to the bottom of the sea? Many ships of the merchant marine have been sunk, our brave sailors drowned, and altogether our shipping faces a grave menace. We should close our embassy in Eire, in protest. It is not in the public interest that we should spend money in a neutral country which is not a British dominion, but doing Hitler's work, and the lights of Dublin and other cities enable Hitler to attack Wales and England.
Further, I believe that we should have a change here with regard to the Vichy government. Let us follow Britain in this matter. We cannot blow hot and cold in these matters. No one knows how many ships of Canadian and British register have been ruined in consequence of lack of proper protection by the right to use these ports in this war, ports which in the war with Napoleon caused damage at the back-door.
Coming to the United States, in connection with this particular vote, which is a large one, I would point out that for nearly two years we have been able to get along without a permanent representative there-almost since the war started. It was a great mistake to open that embassy, because it led to considerable friction between the mother country and the United States before and after the last war. We appreciate all that the people of the United States and their splendid president have done for us, but we must not rely to too great an extent on others. It is safer to rely on ourselves. We must not forget that a year ago we depended upon France and the Maginot line. Everyone said that the Maginot line would hold until Britain and the dominions were prepared, and it failed. We are now depending on the United States for protection this year, as on France last year. I suggest that it would be better for us to depend more on the mother country and on the dominions in the present battle of Britain, both in the old country and in the Mediterranean as help from America may come too late. Mr. Knudsen shocked congress by telling them that it would take two years to get munitions and two years to train men, and in the meantime the war is becoming a grave menace to the empire. No one knows to whom this country will belong even at the end of this year.
I have great respect and admiration for the people of the United States; my respect for them is second to that of no one in this house. At the same time I believe in the policy laid down by Sir John A. Macdonald when he said, speaking in 1844 at a nomination meeting in the city of Kingston, that the present and the future of the people of Canada should always be wrapped up in the mother country, and our maintenance of the British connection forever.
I have been opposed to the policy of giving away air bases. I fail to see why air bases should have been given away from Newfoundland all the way down to British Guiana, bases which the United States have wanted for a hundred years and only got when they found the empire in peril. This move would not have been needed had not the finest army, navy and air force been scrapped in order to please pacifists and those who believe in collective security. An armed Britain would have prevented war. The giving away of these bases has been very much opposed in Britain. Some say that it was done at the suggestion of Canada. If so, then I say that Canada acted with very poor judgment in urging that it should be done; because, after all, the Channel islands and Somaliland have been ceded, and now all the bases from Newfoundland, the key to the St. Lawrence, right down to the gulf of Mexico have been handed over under a ninety-nine year lease-practically a freehold-in exchange for fifty obsolete ships and some munitions up to now paid for on the cash-and-carry plan.
This particular policy will in the end drive Britain	out of	the	western	hemisphere	in	ahundred	years,	and	I am opposed to it	as	apolicy of handing over to the United States parts of our empire to pay for tools. It is not in the interests of the people either of Canada	or of	the	empire	at large, and	I
submit that it has come about as the result of our having separate embassies, and of scrapping the finest army, navy and air force the world ever had, to please the pacifists.
With	regard	to	Rhodes	scholars, I	have
nothing to say against them. In fact, I know most of those from the Canadian universities and I am sure they are good men. But Cecil Rhodes did not intend that the principles which some of them advocate should ever be applied to the empire or expect to see the day when such a separatist drift would start. In my opinion, some politicians sent by us as ambassadors have caused harm in connection with these foreign legations of ours. They do not understand anything about diplomacy and have had no training. A good diplomat never makes speeches but works hard. He sticks to his work like the great men I have named.

Then, what were the qualifications of the former hon. member for Bow River to become secretary of that legation? Why was he appointed to that post? So far as I know, there has been no publicity respecting any of their activities, and I should like to know if at this time when, as the Prime Minister knows, there are grave misgivings respecting the attitude of the government of southern Ireland in connection with the war, they are a useful function of this government.

speechtext:
One of the reasons why Canada has appointed a high commissioner to the Irish Pree State is that the Irish Free State has appointed a high commissioner to Canada. At the time of the appointment by the Irish Free State hope was expressed that Canada might reciprocate. We have felt it wise policy to have representatives in all the other dominions. I believe my hon. friend will agree that, apart from all else, it would have been somewhat invidious if in our representation within the commonwealth, we had left out any one of the dominions.
The reasons, however, for appointing the high commissioner to the Irish Free State were the same as those which prompted us to appoint high commissioners to other parts of the commonwealth, namely, to have some one at the capital of each who would be in touch with members of the government and who would be in a position to bring to the government's attention matters of Canadian concern, and to inform the government in Canada of matters of interest occurring in the country to which the high commissioner may have been sent, also to look after the interests of Canada and Canadians generally.
May I make one or two observations respecting the services rendered by the high commissioner, Mr. Hall Kelly, and the secretary of the legation, Mr. Garland. While publicity has not been given to reports received by our government, the information we have received from that source has been of value. Through the reports we have received from our high commissioner and his secretary we have been in a position to assess the situation in Ireland itself in a manner we would not have found possible had we not had the inside information given us.

speechtext:
It becomes
almost a truism to say that we are going to face difficult days. Speaking in the house only a short time ago, the Prime Minister himself said that experts were agreed that not only was there a possibility of an attempted invasion of Great Britain, but that synchronized with it there was the probability of attacks on Gibraltar and Singapore. No one knows just to what extent the area of the war may spread. Thoughtful people in Canada of necessity must be somewhat concerned, if the war stretches over a large enough area, as to whether or not parts of Canada may be exposed, not so much to the danger of invasion but to the danger of attack by occasional raiders of different sorts.
In view of what I have said, I should like to ask the Prime Minister two questions, knowing that the answers can be given in only a limited way. I should like to know, first, whether the plans for the proposed Alaskan highway have been completed, whether any work has been commenced, and, if so, on what financial basis between Canada and the United States it is being carried out. When will the work be completed?
My second question has reference to the plans formulated by the joint defence board. Again we cannot expect the Prime Minister to make any statement as to where there may be defence projects. I do say, however, that the House of Commons has a right to know that certain plans are being proceeded with. The joint defence board travelled across the country, midst the fanfare of trumpets, and I believe the people would be reassured if they knew the plans were being carried into operation. If they are, we should know something of what the financial arrangements are as between Canada and the United States, whether work has been started or will be commenced in the near future, and approximately what it will cost the Canadian people and the people of the United States of America. Those are twro matters in connection with which the Prime Minister might make a statement. I realize that he must use discretion in giving out information, but he
should be able to tell us enough to assure this committee and the country that adequate steps are being taken to arrange for mutual assistance on the part of Canada and the United States in the event of certain contingencies arising in the near future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO PRICES AND QUANTITIES SOLD SINCE AUGUST 1
speechtext:
I do not know
whether my hon. friend was in the house last evening, but at that time I was asked a similar question and sought to reply. My statement will appear on Hansard of yesterday. I referred to the work of the permanent joint defence board and also to the government's attitude toward disclosing plans which have been recommended by that board. I did not refer specifically to air bases on the route to Alaska, but I might say to my hon. friend that the government is proceeding with the work of establishing bases in accordance with the recommendation of the joint board.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO PRICES AND QUANTITIES SOLD SINCE AUGUST 1
speechtext: I was referring to the Alaska highway rather than to air bases.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO PRICES AND QUANTITIES SOLD SINCE AUGUST 1
speechtext:
Perhaps I
could give what information I have. Pursuant to recommendations of the permanent joint defence board, the Canadian government have arranged to provide suitable landing fields complete with lighting, radio facilities, meteoro'logical equipment and housing for personnel at Grande Prairie, Fort St. John, Fort Nelson, Watson Lake, White Horse, Prince George and Smithers. These fields will provide all the necessary ground facilities for planes travelling from the United States or Canada to Alaska. They will be valuable for commerce as well as for defence purposes.
I have given that statement because it has some bearing on the other matter. The joint board did take into consideration defence problems on the Pacific coast as well as on the Atlantic, and these bases are being established in accordance with the recommendation of the board. The board made no recommendation with respect to the Alaska highway. I believe my hon. friend knows that this matter has been referred to commissions which are inquiring into the matter at the present time.
Both the Canadian government and the United States appointed commissions to examine into this question of the proposed Alaskan highway, and an interim report was made in April, 1940. Since that time further reconnaissance surveys have been made covering possible routes in northern British Columbia and the Yukon territory. A meeting of the Canadian commission is to be held within the next few weeks, which will be followed
Supply-External Affairs

by a joint meeting of the two commissions to consider further the general problem. In the meantime the Canadian government has arrived at no decision as to the advisability or otherwise of constructing the proposed highway.
The other matter raised by my hon. friend had to do with an assurance that definite action was being taken in connection with the recommendations of the permanent joint board. I can give him the most positive assurance on that point. The board has made many recommendations to the government, some of which have been referred to the Department of National Defence, and others to the Department of National Defence for Air and the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. With possibly one exception, and I am not at all sure that that has not been dealt with, all the recommendations, so far as I am able to recall, have been approved by the administration and steps taken to carry them out.
As to financial arrangements between the two countries, that question does not arise because each country makes provision for the work to be done within its own jurisdiction. The work to be done in Canada will be paid for under the War Appropriation Act, and such work as is being done in the United States will be paid for out_ of appropriations by the government of that country. I do not think I need say much more than that. My hon. friend realizes that I cannot refer to particular projects, but I can say that they are quite extensive.
As an illustration of what is being done,
I would refer hon. members to something which evidently has not been noticed by some of their number. At the present time there are United States troops in Newfoundland. They are helping to defend the United States coast if it needs defence, and they are at the very front of our own country. In the event of Newfoundland being invaded, I leave it to the committee to surmise what action they would take. I understood the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) to say that the United States were doing nothing at the present time in connection with this war.
I give this as a concrete example of the kind of steps that are being taken in a very practical way by United States soldiers to take their place at one of the bases, which I thought I heard the hon. member for Broadview say should never have been transferred.

When the house met eight days ago, the Prime Minister tabled the report of the special committee on orientals in British Columbia, which report was dated December, 1940. One recommendation by that committee reads as follows:

That, both for purposes of civil security and in order to deprive persons hostile to the Japanese of a constant and effective ground for complaint, there should be a registration of the Japanese population of British Columbia. (Suggestions for the procedure to be adopted are attached as appendix B.)
The method of reregistration set out in the appendix is that in addition to the information contained on the ordinary registration card for Canadian residents, the cards used for this reregistration should have a space for a small photograph of the holder, together with his description and his national status, whether Canadian born, naturalized or Japanese. It suggests also that the reregistration should be in charge of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. maintopic: QUESTION AS TO PRICES AND QUANTITIES SOLD SINCE AUGUST 1
speechtext: To go back to the Japanese for a moment, would the Prime Minister indicate what steps will be taken to ensure that all Japanese will be registered? It is alleged that a considerable number of Japanese are in British Columbia illegally. I think the number alleged is greater than the actual number. Suppose there may be a comparatively small number, say two or three hundred. A previous investigation indicated that there might be only about one hundred Japanese in British Columbia illegally, but very few steps were taken to remedy that situation. There is now to be another registration, and there will undoubtedly be a number of Japanese who have reason to fear that investigation. Is there any way by which it will be known that every Japanese will be registered? The obvious thing for those Japanese to do who are illegally in the country would be to abstain from registering. What steps will be taken in that regard?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO PRICES AND QUANTITIES SOLD SINCE AUGUST 1
speechtext:
Every Japanese will have to have a registration card to identify him. I doubt very much if any Japanese would be able to continue in any kind of work in British Columbia without having a registration card on his person. Without it he would get into difficulties in short order. The Japanese population in the province would be pretty generally known to the authorities there.
I think I ought also to say this. As my hon. friend knows, there are many of the Japanese nationals who feel very keenly about not being regarded in the same light as other nationals, and they are only too anxious themselves to lend assistance to the federal government in seeing that all Japanese are registered in order to protect their position in the community. They are rendering valuable assistance to the government at the present time in this work.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO PRICES AND QUANTITIES SOLD SINCE AUGUST 1
speechtext:
I can understand that those Japanese who are legally in the country, and they are a large number, will surely make it their business to register, but I cannot conceive that they will go out of their way to give information against those Japanese who have illegally entered the country, because whatever may be the opinion of the Prime Minister or of the government here, we in British Columbia are firmly convinced that "once a Jap always a Jap." The words "being naturalized" are just like a snowflake on a river. It is a mere gesture on the part of the Japanese to secure some privilege such as a fishing licence or something of that kind. The Prime Minister says that they are pretty generally known to the authorities. That might be true where there are twelve
Supply-External Affairs

Japs, let us say, in a village, but it would not be true of a larger place, nearly all Japanese.
The Prime Minister also says that if they were not able to produce a registration card they would not be able to continue in business. In the last war, white men and all others had to be registered, and to make sure all were registered you had to produce your registration card when you bought a railway ticket and other things of that kind. Nothing of that sort so far as I have heard has been recommended in the report of the committee. Those who can qualify will get their registration card, which they will be proud to show as evidence of their all-rightness, but those who are illegally in the country will not go near the place to be registered. Why should they? If, subsequently, they want to purchase a railway ticket or something of that kind and cannot get one without producing a registration card, they will borrow one from a friend. That is a common trick.
There was a regulation made that any Japanese who had served in the great war and could produce his military discharge could get a fishing licence without being subjected to the quota restriction which applied to the ordinary Japanese. What did they do? Every Japanese with a military discharge goes fishing. He does not really. He may be running a cigar store, but he will farm out his fishing licence to another Japanese, who produces the borrowed discharge. They are all alike; you cannot tell one from the other. So it was the practice to peddle out his licence. Every Japanese with a military discharge obtained a fishing licence for some other Japanese. Occasionally they are detected. If it is obvious that they have obtained the licence illegally, it is taken away from them. But that peddling goes on all the time.
I had not intended to bring this subject up at all for various reasons connected with diplomacy and because of the statement which the Prime Minister made earlier in the session, that anyone who made any suggestions dealing with the subject of Japanese in British Columbia was more or less disloyal or at any rate would be regarded as doing it solely for political effect-a thing which some of us in British Columbia do not appreciate.

I wish my hon. friend would quote any statement I made to that effect. He surely has misunderstood the statement I made if he interpreted it as meaning that any member of parliament could not say what he pleased without being regarded as disloyal. I have made no statement of the kind.
fMr. Neill.]

speechtext: I was not prepared to speak on this subject to-night, and I rose only because the subject came up. The Prime Minister's statement will be found in Hansard No. 3, I think, reporting the proceedings on the third day of this session, which began on the 7th of November. The Prime Minister most distinctly stated that he would regard it as highly undesirable if any members made any remarks to excite in any way displeasure with the Japanese. He said he wanted the house to understand it was not just a casual or careless remark which some man might make, because that was not so harmful, as the rest of us knew that such statements were born only of a desire for political effect-it was that remark which I did not like-but that when it went to Japan it was represented as a statement, not of some careless, reckless, unworthy-of-con-fidence man here, but as the decided opinion of the Canadian parliament; and that was what he did not like.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO PRICES AND QUANTITIES SOLD SINCE AUGUST 1
speechtext: May I say to my hon. friend that that is quite different from saying that any hon. member was disloyal. I made no reflection on the loyalty of anyone.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO PRICES AND QUANTITIES SOLD SINCE AUGUST 1
speechtext: Neither did I.
